name: Nora Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the underground crew in the city, so less climbing poles and more climbing down into vaults and trenches. A normal day, we get the job pack at seven at the Eastside yard, drive to wherever a cable's failed, dig or open the vault, find the fault and joint in a new section. Jointing is the part I love, it's careful work, almost like sewing, and you can't rush it. What wears me out is traffic, honestly, and working in a hole with buses going past a metre from your head.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home, and how you got into this.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did an apprenticeship at twenty-three after a few years in a call centre, which I hated. My partner Dev drives the number 14 bus, so between us we know every pothole in the city. We've got Lily, who's fourteen, and Owen, who's ten, and a mortgage on a terraced house near the river. We've got about four months of savings, which feels okay but not great. I'm in the union, I vote left, and I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to translate letters for my mum or check the wording of a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief for most people, and I'd probably share some joke about all the money tech companies burned. At work we'd laugh about the fault-finding app that kept sending us to the wrong street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes. The city still needs its cables jointed, the old lead-covered ones keep failing, and nobody's going to do that from a laptop. If anything I'd be glad the hype didn't give the bosses an excuse to squeeze us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. Maybe use the AI a bit more for paperwork if the company rolls it out properly, because the incident reports take forever. Otherwise, same budget, same overtime, same saving a little each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of 'I told you so' mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the app that sent you to the wrong street.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they gave us a fault-location tool that was meant to read the network and point to the problem. Twice it sent us to Harbour Lane when the fault was two streets over on Quay Road. Our crew leader Hamid just started ignoring it and went back to the old test kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd miss out on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If AI could take the reports off my hands, I'd get home earlier to Owen. So part of me wouldn't mind a little more help than the hype one gives. But I'd want it to help us, not count us.

S0.say: It's a relief for most people, and a bit of a joke about all the money tech companies burned. She'd laugh at work about the fault-finding app that kept sending crews to the wrong street.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for her, because the city's old cables keep failing and nobody joints them from a laptop. She's glad the hype gave bosses no excuse to squeeze the crews.
S0.do: Carries on at the Eastside yard with the same budget, overtime and small monthly saving. Uses AI a little more for incident reports if the company rolls it out properly.
S0.feel: Calm, with a bit of 'I told you so' mixed in.
S0.quote: Twice it sent us to Harbour Lane when the fault was two streets over on Quay Road.
S0.fieldNote: Nora loves the craft of jointing and is quietly sceptical of tools that don't prove themselves. She would actually welcome help with paperwork. Her line that AI should help workers, not count them, came up unprompted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine as long as workers get a say. I'd post in the union group that any new tech should come with training in paid hours and no job losses. And I'd say the savings should go into fixing the network, not bonuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the jointing itself is safe for a while, but the planning and the paperwork get taken over, and that means fewer supervisors and dispatchers. My friend Priya is a dispatcher, and she'd be the one I'd worry about. For me, it probably means learning new kit and being watched more closely by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the company training on whatever they bring in, once a couple of people on the crew have tried it and it works. I'd push the union to negotiate the rollout. And I'd look into the cable testing and diagnostics course at the technical college, because that's where the new skills seem to be going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be paying attention in a way I'm not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by being watched more closely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They already track the vans by GPS. With AI, I can picture a screen telling a manager that my joint took forty minutes longer than average, without knowing the vault was flooded. That kind of thing makes people cut corners, and in our job cutting corners gets you burned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money come from for the testing course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company first, and the union could help with that. If they said no, it's about six hundred for the evening course, and we'd find it out of the holiday fund. Dev would grumble but he'd agree.

S1.say: It's fine as long as workers get a say, with training in paid hours and no job losses. The savings should go into fixing the network, not into bonuses.
S1.think: The jointing is safe for a while, but planning and paperwork get taken over, which hits dispatchers like her friend Priya. For her it means new kit and closer watching by software.
S1.do: Takes the company training once others on the crew have shown the new tools work and pushes the union to negotiate the rollout. Looks into a cable testing and diagnostics evening course, about six hundred, paid by the company or from the holiday fund.
S1.feel: Uneasy, paying attention in a way she isn't now.
S1.quote: That kind of thing makes people cut corners, and in our job cutting corners gets you burned.
S1.fieldNote: Her concern is less about losing the job than about software-driven pressure making the work unsafe. She waits for proof before adopting tools but is willing to pay for a course herself. Her worry extends to a friend in dispatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs an emergency response, like during the pandemic. Wage support for anyone replaced, the energy companies brought into public ownership, and a tax on robot labour. I'd be marching, and I'd make sure Lily came with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it scares me. Underground work is messy and every vault is different, so I'd like to think robots would struggle, but if the card says they can do it, then two years is no time. Four months of savings and a mortgage, with Dev's bus job going too, because buses would drive themselves. Both of us at once is the nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away: no holiday, cancel the streaming, cheaper food shop. Every spare bit goes into savings. I'd get the union to fight for a phased handover and redundancy pay. If we both lost our jobs, I'd go to the council and to Dev's parents, who've got a spare room, and I wouldn't be too proud to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first night after hearing this look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev and I at the kitchen table after the kids are in bed, with a notepad. Working out how long four months really lasts if we stop the gym, the takeaways, Owen's swimming. Probably more like five if we're brutal, and then what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, is there anything you'd try to get ahead of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get onto the robot side, whatever that is, maintaining or supervising the machines. But I'd be competing with every lineworker in the country for those few jobs. Two years is barely enough to finish one course.

S2.say: This needs an emergency response like the pandemic: wage support for anyone replaced, public ownership of energy companies and a tax on robot labour. She'd be marching with her daughter.
S2.think: Two years is no time, and with four months of savings and a mortgage, the real nightmare is Dev's bus job going at the same time as hers. Both incomes at once would sink them.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard at once, dropping the holiday, streaming and Owen's swimming, and puts every spare bit into savings. Gets the union to fight for a phased handover and redundancy pay, and would turn to the council and Dev's parents if both jobs went.
S2.quote: Both of us at once is the nightmare.
S2.fieldNote: The household risk, not her own job alone, drives her alarm: her partner's job is exposed too. She is practical and unashamed about seeking help. She'd try for a robot-maintenance role but sees the competition clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them: retraining funds, a shorter working week, and the energy firms in public hands before the robots arrive, not after. I'd be at the union conference asking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I think I could get myself into one of the jobs that lasts longest, maybe substation protection or testing, where you're the person who signs off that it's safe. Lily would be nineteen, Owen fifteen. I'd still be worried about Dev, but we'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the evening course in protection and testing next September and do the second level the year after. Save an extra two hundred a month and put it all toward six months of cushion. And I'd push our local councillors and whoever's standing in the election on a jobs guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to finish two courses instead of half of one, and time to build the savings. It means I'm not panicking, I'm working through a list. I like a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about Lily's plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She talks about becoming an electrician, and I'd probably nudge her toward something with people in it, like teaching or nursing. That feels awful to say, because she's good with her hands, like me. But I'd want her in something that lasts.

S3.say: There are five years, so use them: retraining funds, a shorter week and public energy firms before the robots arrive. She'd raise it at the union conference.
S3.think: Five years is enough to move into the jobs that last longest, like substation protection and testing, where a person signs off on safety. She still worries about Dev but feels there's time.
S3.do: Starts an evening course in protection and testing next September, with a second level the year after. Saves an extra two hundred a month toward six months of cushion and presses councillors and candidates on a jobs guarantee.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: It means I'm not panicking, I'm working through a list. I like a list.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn her from crisis mode to project mode. She found it painful to imagine steering her daughter away from a trade she'd be good at. Her plan pairs personal retraining with political demands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we don't waste it. We could plan a fair transition properly, with retraining for everyone, a shorter week and some kind of basic income. I'd be campaigning for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd be 53, the kids would be grown, and I could move into testing or teaching apprentices for the years that are left. The thing that'd keep nagging me is whether there'd be anything for the apprentices to do once they finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan as the five-year one, just slower: one course at a time, starting in a year or so once I've seen which skills are holding up. Keep saving steadily. And we'd change the kids' plans a bit, helping Lily look at courses that mix hands-on work with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd sleep. It's a long road, but you can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year before starting. Why wait if you've got the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to see what actually holds up. Like with the fault app, the first version of anything is often rubbish. I'd rather take the course the second wave of people take, when you know it leads somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev about his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to think about what he'd love doing if money weren't the point. He's always said he'd like to coach kids' football. In ten years, maybe that's a real plan rather than a daydream.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if we don't waste it, enough to plan a fair transition with retraining, a shorter week and a basic income. She'd campaign for it.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable: she'd be 53 with grown kids and could move into testing or teaching apprentices. What nags her is whether apprentices would have any work once they finish.
S4.do: Follows the five-year plan more slowly, starting a course in about a year once she sees which skills hold up. Keeps saving steadily and helps Lily look at courses that mix hands-on work with people.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to sleep, with a long road she can see.
S4.quote: I'd rather take the course the second wave of people take, when you know it leads somewhere.
S4.fieldNote: Her steady temperament shows clearly here: she wants proof before committing, even with a decade to spare. Her worry turns outward to the next generation of apprentices. She sees the long runway as a chance for her partner to chase a dream.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Dev and I could both be out at once. What would help is wage support straight away, not after months of forms, and a pause on mortgage payments for people who've been replaced. And real training places, paid, for the jobs that are left.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but if they rush robots into a live network, someone's going to get hurt, maybe a member of the public. I'd want people like me checking the machines' work for a long time.

headlineQuote: I'd want it to help us, not count us.
portrait: Nora Chen is a 43-year-old underground cable jointer in the city, who came to the trade from a call centre and loves the slow, careful work of jointing. She and her partner Dev, a bus driver, have two kids, a mortgage and about four months of savings. She sees mild AI as a paperwork helper, steady change as a matter of union deals and a testing course, and fast AGI as a household emergency because both their jobs would go. With more warning she shifts from alarm to a list-driven plan, but she always waits for proof before she moves.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her partner could lose both incomes at the same time with only four months saved.
whatWouldHelp: Immediate wage support without months of forms, a pause on mortgage payments for replaced workers, and paid training places for the jobs that remain. She also wants experienced workers kept on to check the machines for safety.
